title: RSU Tax Records: What to Keep and How to Read Your Equity Plan Statement
summary: Which RSU records to keep for Indian tax, from vesting and sale to Schedule FA, and how to read the Awards, Positions, Tax Lots and Gain/Loss sections.
body_markdown:
If you receive RSUs from a foreign employer, the documents you need at tax time are spread across your payslips, Form 16 and a stock plan account that most people open only on vest day. The records that matter are few, and almost all of them can be downloaded from that account.


This guide covers what to save each time shares vest, each time you sell and at each year end. It also explains how to read the sections of an equity plan statement, so you know where each number lives.


The reason all of this matters is that RSUs are taxed at two points, on two different amounts. If that is new to you, read[how foreign RSUs are taxed in India](https://paasa.com/blog/how-rsus-are-taxed-in-india) first.


## Table of contents


- Why RSU records matter more than salary records
- How to read your equity plan statement
- Records to keep every time your RSUs vest
- Records to keep every time you sell
- Records to keep for dividends
- Records for Schedule FA: use the calendar year
- What your CA needs, by schedule
- How long to keep RSU records
- Common record-keeping mistakes
- About Paasa


## Why RSU records matter more than salary records


Regular salary is settled within the year. Your employer deducts tax, issues Form 16, and nothing from that year is needed again.


RSUs are different because the value taxed as salary at vesting becomes your cost of acquisition for the capital gains calculation when you sell. That sale may be years later, possibly after you have changed employers or lost access to the old stock plan login.


Each vest is also its own lot. A grant that vests in eight instalments gives you eight lots, each with its own date, cost and holding period, and they cannot be averaged together.


## How to read your equity plan statement


Your stock plan account, whether it runs on Schwab Equity Award Center, Fidelity NetBenefits, Morgan Stanley StockPlan Connect or another platform, holds most of the records in this guide. The section names below are common across platforms but not identical, so treat them as what to look for and not as an exact menu.


Employers also change plan administrators from time to time. Check your own equity plan login to confirm which platform holds your grants.


### 1. Awards: what was granted


This section lists each grant with its grant date, the number of units and the vesting schedule. Refresher grants usually appear as separate awards with their own timelines.


Nothing in the Awards section is taxable. It tells you what is scheduled to vest and when, which is useful for planning advance tax, but a unit matters for tax only once it vests.


### 2. Positions: what you hold today


Positions shows the vested shares sitting in the account right now. It is a snapshot, not a history.


For Indian tax, the total matters less than how it is made up, because each batch of shares arrived on a different date at a different cost.


### 3. Transaction history: the activity log


This is the ledger of everything that has happened in the account: shares credited at vesting, shares sold to cover tax, sales you placed yourself and dividends.


If three tranches vested in a year under sell-to-cover, you should see three deposit entries and a sale entry next to each. Export this section for any period you need to reconstruct, and make sure the export covers the dates you want.


### 4. Tax lots: the record behind your capital gains


This is the section that matters most for your Indian return, and it is easy to overlook. For each lot it typically shows three things.


- **Acquisition date:** the vest date, not the grant date. The holding period for capital gains runs from this date to the date of sale.
- **Quantity:** the shares in that lot, which goes down as you sell from it.
- **Cost basis:** usually the vest-date FMV in dollars. Your Indian cost of acquisition is the rupee value that was taxed as a perquisite, so the dollar figure is a cross-check and not the number you report.


Each lot has its own holding period. Foreign shares held for 24 months or less from the vest date give a short-term gain taxed at your slab rate, and shares held for more than 24 months give a long-term gain taxed at 12.5%.


Lot Vest date Holding period if sold on 15 September 2027 Treatment


Lot 1 1 April 2025 More than 24 months Long-term


Lot 2 1 October 2025 24 months or less Short-term


One sale order can touch both lots, which is why you need each lot's own vest date and cost and not a blended average. For the rates and set-off rules, read[capital gains tax on RSU shares](https://paasa.com/blog/capital-gains-tax-rsu-shares) .


### 5. Gain/Loss report: useful, but built for US rules


This report shows the gain or loss on shares you have sold and often an estimate for shares you still hold. It is in dollars, uses the broker's cost basis and applies the US one-year line between short-term and long-term.


Do not copy its gain figure or its short-term and long-term labels into your Indian return. Use it to confirm quantities, dates and which lot each sale came from.


## Records to keep every time your RSUs vest


Download the vesting confirmation on the day it is issued, so that the record does not depend on your access to the platform later. From it, and from your payslip for that month, record the following for each vest.


- Vest date and number of shares vested
- FMV per share on the vest date
- Number of shares sold or withheld to cover tax, and the price at which they were sold
- Number of shares delivered to your account
- The rupee perquisite value and the TDS shown on your payslip


### Two exchange rates to note


Record two SBI TT buying rates for every vest. The first is the rate on the last day of the month before the month of vesting, which under[Rule 206](https://www.incometaxindia.gov.in/w/rule-206-1) of the Income-tax Rules, 2026 (earlier Rule 115) fixes the perquisite and your cost of acquisition.


The second is the rate on the vest date itself, which Schedule FA uses for the initial value of the investment. Read[SBI TTBR explained](https://paasa.com/blog/sbi-ttbr-rate-explained) for where to find past rates.


### Why Form 16 is not enough


Form 16 shows the total perquisite for the year and the tax deducted on it. It does not break the total into lots, and it says nothing about the shares sold to cover tax, later sales, dividends or year-end holdings.


Keep it together with your vest records and check that the perquisite in Form 16 equals the sum of your own lot values. Read[how to read your Form 16 when you have RSUs](https://paasa.com/blog/form-16-rsu-holders) for that check.


## Records to keep every time you sell


A sale needs its own record, and it must connect back to the vest record of the shares sold. This applies to sales you place yourself and to the shares sold automatically to cover tax at vesting, which are sold in your name and reported in Schedule CG like any other sale.


For each sale, record the following.


- Trade date and number of shares sold
- The vest lot or lots the shares came from, as shown in the trade confirmation or the Gain/Loss report
- Sale price per share and gross proceeds in dollars
- Brokerage, commission or fees charged on the sale
- SBI's TT buying rate on the last day of the month before the month of sale
- Sale proceeds in rupees, the rupee cost of the shares sold and the resulting gain or loss
- Whether the lot was held for 24 months or less, or for more than 24 months


Save the trade confirmation for every sale. If you send the proceeds to India, keep the bank advice for the inward remittance with it.


**Example.** Suppose you are a data engineer in Pune and 60 shares of your US-listed employer vest on 10 September 2025 at an FMV of $200. Your employer sells 21 shares to cover tax, and on 9 March 2026 you sell 20 more at $236. The exchange rates are illustrative, set close to SBI's TT buying rate at the time: ₹88.00 for 31 August 2025 and ₹92.00 for 28 February 2026.


Record Sell-to-cover sale March 2026 sale


Vest lot 10 September 2025 10 September 2025


Shares sold 21 20


Sale price per share $200.40 $236


Exchange rate for the sale ₹88.00 ₹92.00


Sale proceeds in rupees ₹3,70,339 ₹4,34,240


Cost at ₹17,600 per share ₹3,69,600 ₹3,52,000


Holding period 24 months or less 24 months or less


**Short-term capital gain** **₹739** **₹82,240**


### The result: two sale records from one lot, and 19 shares left with a cost of ₹3,34,400


The cost per share of ₹17,600 comes from the vest record: 60 shares × $200 × ₹88.00 gives a perquisite of ₹10,56,000. Without that record, neither gain can be computed, and the 19 shares still held would have no cost on file for a future sale.


## Records to keep for dividends


If your shares pay dividends, record each payment separately.


- Payment date
- Gross dividend in dollars, before any tax
- US tax withheld
- SBI's TT buying rate on the last day of the month before the month in which the dividend was declared or paid


Keep the dividend statement and the year-end tax document your broker issues, such as Form 1042-S. The gross amount goes into your return as income, and the tax withheld supports your foreign tax credit claim. Read[how dividend income from RSU shares is taxed](https://paasa.com/blog/dividend-income-from-rsu-shares-taxed) for the calculation.


## Records for Schedule FA: use the calendar year


Your US statement runs from January to December. Your Indian return runs from April to March for salary and capital gains. Schedule FA, the part of the return where foreign assets are disclosed, follows the calendar year.


So the return for FY 2025-26 reports salary and gains for 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026, and foreign assets held at any time between 1 January 2025 and 31 December 2025. A lot that vested in February 2025 is outside that financial year for salary, but inside that calendar year for Schedule FA.


For each calendar year, download the following.


- The January to December account statement
- A holdings statement as on 31 December, with the share price on that date
- The transaction history for the same twelve months, showing vests, sales and dividends


From these, each vest lot needs its vest date, its initial value, the highest value it reached during the year and its value on 31 December, along with sale proceeds and dividends for the year. Note the SBI TT buying rate for the vest date, the peak date and 31 December, since Schedule FA converts each value on its own date. The account itself is reported separately from the shares.


Shares sold before 31 December still have to be disclosed for that year, with a closing value of nil. This includes sell-to-cover shares that your statement shows were delivered to you and then sold, so note for each vest whether the shares for tax were sold after delivery or withheld before it. Unvested RSUs are not disclosed, because they are not yours until they vest.


Schedule FA applies only to taxpayers who are resident and ordinarily resident. Leaving it out can attract a penalty of ₹10 lakh under the Black Money Act, which does not apply where your foreign assets other than immovable property total ₹20 lakh or less. Read[Schedule FA for RSU holders](https://paasa.com/blog/schedule-fa-rsu-holders) for how each value is worked out.


## What your CA needs, by schedule


This is the one list to hand over at filing time.


Part of the return Records to share Where they come from


Salary (Schedule S) Form 16, Form 12BA, payslips for vest months, vesting confirmations Employer and stock plan account


Capital gains (Schedule CG) Lot-wise vest record, trade confirmations for every sale including sell-to-cover, fees, the exchange rate for each sale Tax Lots, Transaction history, your own sheet


Foreign assets (Schedule FA) January to December statement, 31 December holdings, vest dates and values per lot Positions and Transaction history, calendar-year view


Dividends and foreign tax credit (Schedule OS, FSI, TR and Form 67) Dividend statements, Form 1042-S or other proof of tax withheld Stock plan or brokerage account


Cross-check Form 26AS and AIS Income tax e-filing portal


Form 67 becomes Form 44 from Tax Year 2026-27, and Form 16 becomes Form 130. To see where each of these numbers is entered, follow the[ITR-2 walkthrough for RSUs](https://paasa.com/blog/how-to-file-itr-for-foreign-rsus) .


## How long to keep RSU records


Keep the vest record of a lot until every share from it has been sold and that sale has been reported in your return. For shares you hold for many years, that means keeping vest records for many years.


Two things extend this. A capital loss can be carried forward for eight years if the return was filed on time, so keep the sale records behind a loss for as long as you are carrying it. Schedule FA is filed every year you hold the shares, so keep each calendar-year statement with the return it supported.


If you plan to move your shares to another broker or leave your employer, download the full history from the stock plan account first. Once an account is closed or transferred, you cannot count on getting old documents from it.


## Common record-keeping mistakes


- **Not downloading vesting confirmations.** They are the source of your cost, and you may no longer have the stock plan login when you sell years later.
- **Mixing vest lots.** Each lot has its own cost and holding period, and an average of several lots gives the wrong gain.
- **Ignoring the shares sold to cover tax.** They are part of your perquisite and also a sale of their own.
- **Saving only one exchange rate.** The month-end rate fixes your cost, and the vest-date rate is needed for Schedule FA.
- **Copying the broker's Gain/Loss figures.** They follow US rules and are in dollars.
- **Pulling the financial-year view for Schedule FA.** The schedule needs January to December.
- **Relying only on Form 16.** It has the salary side and nothing else.
